Zack Snyder's Justice League

Four hours. That is what Zack Snyder needed to tell this story properly, and for once in the history of the superhero blockbuster, a studio let a director find out if he was right.

✅ NOT A WOKE TRAP

Zack Snyder's Justice League does not qualify as a woke trap under VVWS v1.1. The film carries a +17.72 TRAD margin and a TRADITIONAL verdict. Its woke-adjacent signals are visible from early in the film: Wonder Woman's combat superiority, Cyborg's backstory involving dehumanization by a Silas Stone figure who prioritized science over his son's consent. None of this is concealed past the 50% mark. The film's overwhelming traditional architecture, messianic resurrection, brotherhood of protectors, masculine redemption, and good triumphing over absolute evil, is present and consistent from first frame to last. No trap. Just a very long, very traditional film with a few genre-standard diversity signals.

Our Verdict on Zack Snyder's Justice League

Four hours. That is what Zack Snyder needed to tell this story properly, and for once in the history of the superhero blockbuster, a studio let a director find out if he was right.

He was right.

Zack Snyder's Justice League is the most complete argument for what the DCEU could have been, assembled from Snyder's original footage after his departure from the theatrical cut following his daughter's death in 2017. It is, among other things, a film shaped by grief, and you can feel that in its relationship to resurrection. Superman comes back. The word that keeps appearing in the film is 'unity.' Unity of purpose. Unity of power. Unity of sacrifice.

The film has six heroes and gives each of them something real to do. That is its first achievement. The theatrical Whedon cut, 119 minutes long and operating under instructions to be lighter and faster, gutted Cyborg's arc almost entirely and reduced several characters to cameos. The Snyder Cut restores all of it. What you get is a film where each character's reasons for being there matter to the story.

Bruce Wayne's arc is redemption. He believed in nothing after Superman's death. He spent the gap between films constructing a team not because he believed they would win but because he believed they had to try. His faith in people is rebuilt over four hours. By the end he is the man who charges into battle against a god-level threat because someone has to go first, and he has decided to be that someone. Ben Affleck has never been better.

Victor Stone / Cyborg is the heart of the film. Snyder said this explicitly and it is true. Victor is a young man who was dying in a car crash and whose father used a Mother Box, alien technology, to rebuild him without his consent. He survived. He resents surviving. He lives in isolation, monitoring financial systems, occasionally moving money to people who need it, doing good anonymously from behind a wall of rejection. His journey in this film is the same journey as Clark Kent's in Man of Steel: accepting what you are and deciding to use it in service of others rather than hiding it out of shame. Ray Fisher plays this with restraint and genuine sadness. It is the best acting in the film.

Superman's resurrection is the sequence most divisive among viewers. When Clark comes back, he comes back wrong. Black suit, red eyes briefly appearing, no memory, no restraint. Batman, Wonder Woman, Aquaman, Cyborg, and The Flash fight him in what might be the most genuinely frightening superhero fight ever filmed, because one side does not want to hurt the other and the other side is not holding back. It resolves through Lois Lane, which is either the most dramatically efficient solution or the laziest one depending on your patience. I find it efficient. The woman who understands his humanity is the only thing that can reach his humanity when his mind has gone dark. That is not lazy. That is internally consistent.

Steppenwolf is not a great villain. He is a tool of Darkseid rather than an independent threat, and the film is honest about this: everything Steppenwolf does is in service of reclaiming his place at Darkseid's side after a previous failure. He has no ideology beyond conquest and no inner life beyond fear of his master. As an antagonist this makes him structurally useful, because the fight against him is really a fight against what he represents: the ancient evil that has been trying to absorb Earth's identity into itself since the age of gods and men. Snyder's real villain is Darkseid, seen briefly and left for unmade sequels. That the sequels were never made is the primary artistic failing attached to this film from the outside.

The epilogue Knightmare sequence is the film's structural weakness. It introduces Jared Leto's Joker, shows a world where Superman has fallen to Darkseid's Anti-Life Equation, and features appearances by Mera, Deathstroke, and others in a dark future Batman is trying to prevent. It is compelling as a teaser. As an ending to a four-hour film that already ended fifteen minutes earlier, it asks more of the viewer than the film has earned. Whether you find it exciting or frustrating depends on how much you trusted that the sequels were coming.

They were not. This is all there is. Given that: it is enough.

Creative Team Deep Dive

Director: Zack Snyder

TRADITIONAL LEANING. See Man of Steel and Batman v Superman reviews for full profile. The Snyder Cut of Justice League is the fullest expression of Snyder's creative vision for the DCEU, assembled after personal tragedy (the death of his daughter Autumn), released after a years-long fan campaign, and constructed as an act of artistic completion rather than commercial calculation. The result is more emotionally transparent than his previous films. The Cyborg arc, which Joss Whedon's theatrical cut largely gutted, is the most personal section of the film: a son whose body was changed without his consent by a father who thought he was saving him, who must decide whether what was done to him can be integrated into his identity or whether it defines him. Snyder has said this arc is the heart of the film. The traditional reading of it is that Cyborg chooses to use what was done to him for good, turning violation into protection. That is the oldest shape of masculine redemption.

Zack Snyder's Justice League arrived in March 2021 under the most unusual circumstances in blockbuster history. Snyder had departed the original Justice League production in 2017 following his daughter's suicide. Warner Bros. replaced him with Joss Whedon, who reshot approximately 25% of the film and delivered a 119-minute theatrical cut that was widely received as a significant downgrade. The fan campaign to release the Snyder Cut, #ReleaseTheSnyderCut, became a years-long cultural event. When HBO Max committed to releasing it, Snyder was given roughly $70 million to complete and expand the film. The result is 4 hours and 2 minutes long, shot in a 1.33:1 aspect ratio for 4K television, and represents Snyder's intended vision without the compromises that would have been required for theatrical release. The film is not flawless. At four hours, certain sequences that would have been trimmed for theatrical release remain. The epilogue 'Knightmare' sequence adds material that points toward sequels that will likely never be made. But as a complete artistic statement, it is more coherent and more emotionally resonant than any version of Justice League that preceded it.

Content Breakdown

Adult Viewer Insight

The Snyder Cut arrived at a specific cultural moment: March 2021, more than a year into a pandemic that had eliminated theatrical cinema as the primary delivery mechanism for blockbuster mythology. HBO Max needed content. The #ReleaseTheSnyderCut campaign, which had sustained itself for four years, provided both the audience and the goodwill. The release became an event not because of its marketing but because of what it represented: a director who had been overruled getting the last word. For VirtueVigil readers, the most interesting question about the Snyder Cut is what it says about how ideology works in franchise filmmaking. Joss Whedon's theatrical cut was, by most accounts, actively hostile to Snyder's material: it inserted quip-driven humor, lightened the tone, and eliminated the darkness that had defined the DCEU. Whedon's cut of Wonder Woman's opening sequence cut a female villain; his version of The Flash included a scene where Barry Allen falls face-first into Iris West's chest. The Snyder Cut removed all of that. The resulting film is not 'feminist' in any recognizable progressive sense. It is mythological in the oldest sense: heroes with specific virtues gathering to defeat an ancient evil because the world will end if they do not. That framework, the fellowship of protectors, the sacrifice required to stop darkness from consuming civilization, is among the most traditional available. Cyborg's arc deserves separate attention. The reading of Cyborg as a woke signal is understandable: a Black character whose institutional failure narrative (his father prioritized his experiment over his son's consent) has racial resonance. The traditional reading is more accurate. Victor Stone is a man who was wounded by the world and chose to protect it anyway. That is the oldest masculine redemption template. The institutional critique in his backstory is parental, not systemic: one father who made a wrong choice, who eventually recognizes it, and whose son must decide whether forgiveness is possible. That is not a progressive story. That is the oldest story about fathers and sons.

Parental Guidance

Rated R for violence and some language. At four hours, this film is inappropriate for young children regardless of content. For mature teenagers 15 and up, it is the most complete version of the DCEU mythology and worth the investment. The violence is significant but purposeful. The themes of sacrifice, redemption, the cost of grief, and the choice to protect others regardless of personal cost are genuinely worth discussing. Superman's resurrection sequence may require context for viewers who have not seen Batman v Superman. The epilogue teases sequels that were never made, which is worth knowing before you watch.
